source_refs.note: Topic 24.3.3 with Quick Check 24.4, answered (PDF 124-126). The book labels the methyl orange product 'p-dimethylaminoazobenzene' and draws it with N triple bond N; the lesson names it methyl orange (-N=N-). The coupling mechanism and photographs are summarised. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Phenylamine gives two types of reaction: those of the benzene ring and those of the -NH2 group. The ring carbons are sp2 hybridised and the nitrogen is sp3 hybridised.

The amino group is ortho-para directing and makes the benzene ring very reactive, especially at these positions. Bromination of phenylamine is therefore faster than that of benzene, and both ortho positions and the para position are substituted in a single reaction, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine: C6H5NH2 + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3NH2 + 3HBr.
b) With nitrous acid: diazonium salts

Phenylamine, a primary amine, reacts with nitrous acid to form a diazonium salt; this is diazotisation. Compounds with the diazonium group, -N2+ (written -N+ triple bond N), are diazo compounds. Nitrous acid is made in situ from sodium nitrite and HCl, and the mixture is kept below 10 C with ice, because diazonium salts are unstable and decompose easily, giving off nitrogen, even at room temperature: C6H5NH2 + HNO2 + HCl -> C6H5N2+ Cl- + 2H2O (below 10 C). On warming with water the salt gives phenol: C6H5N2+ Cl- + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl.

Alkyl diazonium salts are highly unstable under all conditions and cannot be isolated, but aryl diazonium salts are fairly stable at low temperatures. The extra stability comes from the delocalisation of the positive charge over the aromatic ring. Benzenediazonium salts are important intermediates in making many organic compounds.

blocks.alt: Top: phenylamine + 3Br2 gives 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine + 3HBr; NH2 activates the ring and directs to 2, 4 and 6. Bottom: phenylamine + HNO2 + HCl below 10 C gives benzenediazonium chloride + 2H2O; benzenediazonium chloride + H2O on warming gives phenol + N2 + HCl. A note says aryl diazonium ions are stable in the cold because their charge is delocalised over the ring.
blocks.caption: Bromination and diazotisation of phenylamine (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: Like phenol, phenylamine reacts with bromine water without a catalyst. With cold nitrous acid its -NH2 group becomes a diazonium group, -N2+; on warming, nitrogen gas is lost and the ring carbon takes an -OH group from water.

blocks.text: Aryl diazonium salts react with strongly activated aromatic compounds such as phenols and amines; these are coupling reactions, and their products, containing an -N=N- bond, are azo compounds. The positively charged diazonium ion acts as an electrophile and substitutes into the ring of phenol at the para position. Coupling with phenol occurs in mild alkaline solution, and with aromatic amines in mild acid: C6H5N2+ Cl- + C6H5OH -> C6H5-N=N-C6H4OH + HCl (NaOH), giving 4-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange solid.

items: Butter yellow: benzenediazonium chloride couples with N,N-dimethylphenylamine in ethanoic acid to give 4-dimethylaminoazobenzene. It was once used in food but is now forbidden because it can cause cancer.
Methyl orange, an acid-base indicator, is made from diazotised sulphanilic acid and N,N-dimethylphenylamine.

The azo group (Ar-N=N-Ar) is a chromophore: it is responsible for the intense colours of azo dyes, from yellow and orange to red, blue and green, depending on the other groups on the rings. Many food colours contain azo dyes.

blocks.alt: Top: the benzenediazonium ion + phenol in cold NaOH gives 4-hydroxyazobenzene, Ph-N=N-C6H4-OH, an orange solid; the diazonium ion attacks the para position. Middle: C6H5N2+ Cl- + C6H5N(CH3)2 gives butter yellow, C6H5-N=N-C6H4-N(CH3)2 + HCl. Bottom: diazotised sulphanilic acid + N,N-dimethylphenylamine gives methyl orange; the -N=N- chromophore gives azo dyes their colour.
blocks.caption: Coupling reactions and azo dyes (original diagram after the book's equations and mechanism).
blocks.long_description: In a coupling reaction the diazonium ion is the electrophile and the activated ring of phenol or of an aromatic amine is attacked, at the position opposite the OH or N(CH3)2 group. The product keeps the -N=N- link between two aromatic rings; this long delocalised system absorbs visible light, so azo compounds are strongly coloured.
